title: The Chain and Its Weakest Link
topic: trophic cascades and the difficulty of proving them
paragraphs: Remove a predator from a community and the effects should ripple down through everything it ate and everything its prey ate.
Ecologists call this a trophic cascade: a top predator's influence tumbles down through two or more feeding levels, the sign of the effect flipping at each step.
More predators mean fewer grazers, and fewer grazers mean more plants.
It is one of ecology's most satisfying ideas, simple to state and, in a few famous cases, demonstrated with something close to proof.
Yet the cleaner a cascade story sounds, the more tempting it is to tell it without checking whether every link actually held.
The first of those cases began in 1963 on a rocky shore at Mukkaw Bay, on the outer coast of Washington's Olympic Peninsula.

Robert Paine, a zoologist at the University of Washington, began removing every ochre sea star, Pisaster ochraceus, from a section of intertidal rock, prying them loose and flinging them into deeper water.
A neighboring stretch of shore, left alone, served as the control.
The sea star is the main predator of the California mussel, and without it the mussels spread downward across rock that had held barnacles, limpets, chitons, and algae.
Within a few years the mussels had crowded most of these out, and the species count on the cleared plot fell from about fifteen to eight.
Paine published the result in 1966.
In 1969 Paine gave the pattern a name that has stuck: the keystone species.
The metaphor comes from the wedge-shaped block at the top of an arch, small relative to the whole but holding every other stone in place.
A keystone predator is one whose effect on its community is far out of proportion to its abundance.
The sea stars were never numerous, but their steady predation arrested the mussels' advance and kept space open for everything else.

The method mattered more than the metaphor: Paine had not merely observed a correlation; he had removed the predator, watched the response, and compared it against an untouched plot a few meters away.
In 1980 Paine also supplied the phrase "trophic cascade" itself.
The second case came from the Aleutian Islands of Alaska, where James Estes began studying sea otters in the early 1970s.
The fur trade had hunted otters nearly to extinction, and when an international treaty protected them in 1911 only scattered remnant colonies survived.
By the 1970s the otters had recovered around some islands but not others, which gave Estes a natural comparison.
Around islands with otters, the sea floor was a forest of kelp.
Around islands without them, the kelp was gone and the rock was carpeted with sea urchins, a condition divers call an urchin barren.
Sea otters eat urchins, urchins eat kelp, and so a predator two links away determines whether a kelp forest exists at all.
Estes and a colleague published the comparison in Science in 1974.
The otter story later acquired a fourth link nobody had planned for.

In the 1990s, otter numbers around the western Aleutians collapsed, and in 1998 Estes and his colleagues reported that killer whales had apparently begun eating otters, possibly because their usual prey of seals and sea lions had declined.
As the otters vanished, urchins returned and the kelp thinned again.
This is perhaps the most instructive part of the story: a cascade is not a closed loop but an open chain, and a disturbance anywhere along it can be felt on the rocks near shore.
No cascade story is told more often than the Yellowstone wolf story, and none is harder to pin down.
Gray wolves had been eliminated from Yellowstone National Park by the 1920s.
In 1995 biologists released fourteen wolves captured in Alberta, and in 1996 they added seventeen more from British Columbia, for a total of thirty-one founders.
By then the northern range elk herd numbered nearly twenty thousand, and the willows, aspen, and cottonwoods along the streams had been browsed to stubs for decades.
Within a few years, William Ripple and Robert Beschta of Oregon State University reported that young willows and aspen in parts of the northern range were taller than they had been in decades.
Their explanation had two parts.
First, wolves were killing elk, so there were fewer mouths to browse the shoots.
Second, the surviving elk were afraid, avoiding streamside thickets and valley bottoms where wolves could ambush them, so plants in those risky places got a reprieve.

From there the story grew: taller willows would bring back beavers, beaver dams would raise water tables and create wetlands, songbirds would return, and stabilized banks would change the shape of the rivers.
In 2014 a short video titled "How Wolves Change Rivers," narrated by the British writer George Monbiot, carried this version to tens of millions of viewers.
Almost every piece of that account has since been contested, and the contest is where the lessons lie.
Elk numbers did fall, from nearly twenty thousand in the mid-1990s to a few thousand by the 2010s.
But wolves were far from the only new pressure.
Hunters in Montana took more than a thousand elk in some winters as the herd migrated north out of the park.
Grizzly bears and black bears, both increasing, took a large share of newborn calves each spring.
Cougars had quietly recolonized the park in the 1980s.
A severe drought in the early 2000s reduced the forage elk depend on.
Sorting the wolves' share out of that list is an accounting problem no one has fully solved.
The second half of the hypothesis, the idea that fear alone reshaped elk behavior, has fared worse.

The phrase "landscape of fear" was introduced in 2001 to describe how Yellowstone's elk and bison might read the terrain for danger, and it was quickly adopted as the mechanism behind the plant recovery.
But when Matthew Kauffman and colleagues tested it in 2010, aspen stands where elk faced the highest risk from wolves were recovering no better than stands in safer places.
Tracking-collar studies found that an individual elk met wolves only occasionally and went back to feeding soon afterward, hardly the behavior of an animal too frightened to eat.
Then there is the matter of water, which the tidy version leaves out entirely.

Willows along Yellowstone's small streams need a high water table, and the beavers whose dams once maintained it had been nearly absent for decades, partly because there were no tall willows for them to eat and build with.
A decade-long experiment by Colorado State University researchers fenced willow plots to keep elk out and, in some, built small dams to mimic the work of beavers.
Willows protected from browsing but left with a low water table did not reach the heights of the past, while those given both protection and water did.
Removing the browsers is not enough: the willows need the beavers and the beavers need the willows, a loop that wolves alone cannot restart.
The claim that wolves changed the course of rivers is the boldest in the chain and rests on the thinnest evidence.
Stream channels were cut deep by decades of erosion while the willows were gone, and channel form responds to vegetation over spans far longer than the twenty years since the wolves returned.
The change in the rivers that the video describes remains a projection more than a measured result.
None of this means the wolves did nothing.
Elk are fewer, some willow stands have recovered, and biologists still argue over how much credit the wolves deserve, which is exactly how a live scientific question should look.
What separates Yellowstone from Mukkaw Bay or the Aleutians is not the strength of the idea but the shape of the evidence.
Paine had a control plot, and Estes had islands with and without otters.
Yellowstone is a single reintroduction in a single park, with bears, cougars, hunters, drought, and beavers all changing at once, and nothing to compare it against.
The trophic cascade remains one of ecology's best ideas, and the honest way to admire it is to keep asking, at every link, whether the chain was tested or merely assumed.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happened on the plot at Mukkaw Bay after the sea stars were removed?
choices: Barnacles replaced the mussels as the dominant animal on the rock
The number of species fell from about fifteen to eight
Kelp spread across rock that the mussels had once held
Sea urchins carpeted the rock once the sea stars were gone
The number of species roughly doubled as the mussels spread

proof.quote: the species count on the cleared plot fell from about fifteen to eight

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says that once the mussels crowded the other species out, the species count on the cleared plot fell from about fifteen to eight.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the mussels crowded out the barnacles, not the other way around.
Kelp belongs to the Aleutian otter story in paragraph 4, not to Mukkaw Bay.
Urchin barrens are the Aleutian result in paragraph 4; at Mukkaw Bay the mussels took over.
Reversed: diversity fell by about half, it did not double.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 3, the word 'arrested' most nearly means
choices: detained
captured
halted
attracted
punished

proof.quote: their steady predation arrested the mussels' advance

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the predation 'arrested the mussels' advance and kept space open,' so the sea stars were stopping the mussels from spreading. The police meaning of the word is the trap.
distractorNotes: The police sense of the word; sea stars do not detain mussels.
Sea stars do eat mussels, but the sentence is about stopping the mussels' advance, not seizing individuals.
Opposite in spirit; the predation held the mussels back rather than drawing them in.
Imports a moral sense the sentence does not carry.

questions.stem: The author mentions 'an untouched plot a few meters away' in paragraph 3 primarily to
choices: show how small the area Paine studied actually was
explain why the mussels spread downward across the rock
suggest that the sea stars soon recolonized the cleared rock
stress that Paine's result rested on an experiment with a control
argue that sea star removal had effects well beyond the boundaries of the cleared plot

proof.quote: compared it against an untouched plot a few meters away

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the method mattered more than the metaphor: Paine had not merely observed a correlation; he removed the predator and compared the result against an untouched plot. The untouched plot is the control, and that is the point being made.
distractorNotes: The distance is not there to describe the study's size; the sentence is about method.
The mussels' spread is explained in paragraph 2 by the missing predator, not by the control plot.
The passage never says the sea stars recolonized the plot.
Nothing in the passage describes effects spilling outside the cleared plot.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following characterized Aleutian islands that lacked sea otters?
choices: Rock carpeted with sea urchins and stripped of kelp
Kelp forests that had grown unusually dense in the otters' absence
Remnant otter colonies protected by the 1911 treaty
Killer whales feeding on seals and sea lions
Mussel beds that crowded out other species

proof.quote: the kelp was gone and the rock was carpeted with sea urchins

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says that around islands without otters 'the kelp was gone and the rock was carpeted with sea urchins,' which divers call an urchin barren.
distractorNotes: Reversed: kelp forests were found around islands with otters, not without them.
Remnant colonies are where otters survived; the question asks about islands without them.
Killer whales enter in paragraph 5, and their switch to otters is a 1990s event, not a feature of otter-free islands in the 1970s.
Mussel beds are the Mukkaw Bay result in paragraph 2.

questions.stem: The passage implies that Estes's study differed from Paine's in that Estes
choices: removed the predator from the study area himself
worked without any site to compare against
studied a predator that was more numerous than the sea star
published his results before the term keystone species existed
relied on a comparison he had not set up himself

proof.quote: which gave Estes a natural comparison
Paine had a control plot, and Estes had islands with and without otters

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says uneven otter recovery 'gave Estes a natural comparison,' and paragraph 12 contrasts Paine's control plot with Estes's islands. Paine created his comparison; nature handed Estes his.
distractorNotes: That describes Paine, who pried the sea stars loose by hand.
The islands with and without otters were his comparison.
The passage says nothing about how numerous otters were relative to sea stars.
Keystone species was named in 1969; Estes published in 1974.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Estes and his colleagues reported in 1998 that
choices: sea otters had been protected by a new international treaty
urchin barrens around the western Aleutians had turned back into kelp forest
killer whales had apparently begun to eat sea otters
seals and sea lions had recovered around the western Aleutians
sea otters had spread to the shore at Mukkaw Bay

proof.quote: killer whales had apparently begun eating otters

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the 1998 report was that 'killer whales had apparently begun eating otters,' possibly because seals and sea lions had declined.
distractorNotes: The treaty dates to 1911, in paragraph 4.
Reversed: as otters vanished, urchins returned and the kelp thinned.
Reversed: the passage suggests seals and sea lions had declined, not recovered.
Mukkaw Bay is Paine's sea star site; otters are never placed there.

questions.stem: The author describes the killer whale episode in paragraph 5 primarily to
choices: show that the sea otter cascade had been mistaken all along
explain why the fur trade nearly drove sea otters to extinction
argue that killer whales deserve the label keystone species
show that a cascade is an open chain, not a closed loop
demonstrate that kelp forests recover quickly once urchin numbers fall

proof.quote: a cascade is not a closed loop but an open chain

questions.why: Paragraph 5 calls the episode 'the most instructive part of the story' because it shows 'a cascade is not a closed loop but an open chain' that a disturbance from elsewhere can reach.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the episode extends the cascade by a link; it does not overturn it.
The fur trade is in paragraph 4 and has nothing to do with killer whales.
The passage never applies the keystone label to killer whales.
Reversed: when the otters vanished, the kelp thinned.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how many wolves in total were released in Yellowstone in 1995 and 1996?
choices: fourteen
seventeen
twenty
thirty-one
nearly twenty thousand

proof.quote: for a total of thirty-one founders

questions.why: Paragraph 6 gives fourteen wolves in 1995 and seventeen in 1996, 'for a total of thirty-one founders.'
distractorNotes: Fourteen is the 1995 release alone.
Seventeen is the 1996 release alone.
Twenty does not appear in the passage; it is a rough mental sum that misses by eleven.
Nearly twenty thousand is the size of the elk herd, not the number of wolves.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Ripple and Beschta's explanation for the taller willows and aspen had which two parts?
choices: Fewer elk overall, and surviving elk that avoided risky places
Drought on the northern range and the return of beavers to its streams
Human hunting north of the park and rising bear predation on calves
Higher water tables and fewer cougars in the valley bottoms
Beaver dams and the return of songbirds to the thickets

proof.quote: wolves were killing elk, so there were fewer mouths to browse the shoots
the surviving elk were afraid, avoiding streamside thickets and valley bottoms

questions.why: Paragraph 7 lays out the two parts: wolves killed elk so there were fewer mouths to browse, and the surviving elk were afraid and avoided streamside thickets and valley bottoms.
distractorNotes: Drought and beavers belong to the critics' side in paragraphs 8 and 10, not to Ripple and Beschta's explanation.
Hunting and bears are alternative pressures from paragraph 8, raised by critics, not by Ripple and Beschta.
Water tables are part of the Colorado State experiment in paragraph 10; cougars appear in paragraph 8.
These are downstream predictions in the extended story, not the two-part explanation itself.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 7, the extended version of the Yellowstone story predicted all of the following EXCEPT
choices: the return of beavers to the streams
the return of songbirds
stabilized stream banks
rivers changing shape
a decline in grizzly bears

proof.quote: taller willows would bring back beavers
songbirds would return
stabilized banks
change the shape of the rivers

questions.why: Paragraph 7 lists beavers, wetlands, songbirds, stabilized banks, and reshaped rivers. Bears appear only in paragraph 8, and there they are increasing, not declining.
distractorNotes: Stated: 'taller willows would bring back beavers.'
Stated: 'songbirds would return.'
Stated: 'stabilized banks would change the shape of the rivers.'
Stated: the banks 'would change the shape of the rivers.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the popular version of the Yellowstone story is best described as
choices: admiring
skeptical
indifferent
hostile
bewildered

proof.quote: which the tidy version leaves out entirely
the boldest in the chain and rests on the thinnest evidence
without checking whether every link actually held

questions.why: The judging words are 'tidy version,' 'boldest in the chain,' 'thinnest evidence,' and 'a projection more than a measured result.' That is doubt with reasons, not dismissal.
distractorNotes: The author admires the cascade idea and Paine's method, not the popular Yellowstone retelling.
An indifferent writer would not spend five paragraphs testing the story link by link.
Too strong: the author says 'none of this means the wolves did nothing.'
The author is not confused; the critique is organized and specific.

questions.stem: All of the following are mentioned in the passage as pressures on Yellowstone's elk other than wolves EXCEPT
choices: hunting by people north of the park in Montana
predation on newborn calves by bears
the recolonization of the park by cougars
a severe drought in the early 2000s
disease spreading from domestic cattle

proof.quote: Hunters in Montana took more than a thousand elk
took a large share of newborn calves
Cougars had quietly recolonized the park
A severe drought in the early 2000s

questions.why: Paragraph 8 lists hunters, bears, cougars, and drought. Disease never appears anywhere in the passage.
distractorNotes: Stated: hunters in Montana took more than a thousand elk in some winters.
Stated: grizzly and black bears took a large share of newborn calves.
Stated: cougars had recolonized the park in the 1980s.
Stated: a severe drought in the early 2000s reduced forage.

questions.stem: The passage implies that if the 'landscape of fear' had been the main driver of plant recovery, then
choices: aspen in risky places should have outgrown aspen in safe ones
elk numbers would have needed to fall below a few thousand
beavers would have returned before the willows grew tall
the wolves would have had to come from Alberta rather than British Columbia
the drought of the early 2000s would have had no effect on elk

proof.quote: aspen stands where elk faced the highest risk from wolves were recovering no better than stands in safer places

questions.why: Paragraph 9 treats Kauffman's finding, that high-risk aspen stands were 'recovering no better than stands in safer places,' as evidence against the fear hypothesis. That only counts against it if the hypothesis predicted the risky stands would do better.
distractorNotes: The fear hypothesis is about behavior, not a threshold in elk numbers.
The passage says beavers need tall willows first, the opposite order.
Where the wolves came from has no bearing on the fear mechanism.
Nothing links the fear hypothesis to drought having no effect.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Colorado State University experiment found that willows grew to the heights of the past only when they were
choices: left unfenced but given a raised water table
fenced and also given a raised water table
fenced after live beavers had been returned to the streams
browsed lightly by elk during the winter months
fenced from elk but left with a low water table

proof.quote: those given both protection and water did

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says willows protected from browsing but left with a low water table did not reach the heights of the past, 'while those given both protection and water did.'
distractorNotes: Half right: water alone is not what the passage credits; the successful plots had fences as well.
The experiment used small built dams to mimic beavers, not live beavers.
Light browsing is never mentioned; the fences kept elk out.
This is the group that did not reach the past heights.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the claim about rivers is weak chiefly because
choices: the rivers in the northern range have changed in the opposite direction
beavers have never returned to any Yellowstone stream
stream channels respond more slowly than twenty years
the video that popularized it was narrated by a writer rather than a scientist
elk never browsed close enough to the rivers to affect them

proof.quote: channel form responds to vegetation over spans far longer than the twenty years since the wolves returned

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says channel form 'responds to vegetation over spans far longer than the twenty years since the wolves returned,' which is why the river change is called a projection rather than a measured result.
distractorNotes: The passage says the change is unmeasured, not that it ran the other way.
Too strong and unsupported: the passage never says beavers are absent from every stream.
The author never attacks Monbiot's credentials; the objection is about evidence and time.
Reversed: the passage says willows along the streams had been browsed to stubs for decades.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the kind of evidence the author says Yellowstone lacks?
choices: Removing a fish from some ponds and leaving matched ponds untouched
Noting that deer declined in a park during the decade after coyotes arrived there
Filming a documentary about how sharks protect seagrass meadows
Counting the birds in a single forest over one summer
Building a computer model of plant growth after predators return

proof.quote: Paine had a control plot, and Estes had islands with and without otters
nothing to compare it against

questions.why: Paragraph 12 says what Yellowstone lacks is a comparison: Paine had a control plot and Estes had islands with and without otters. Ponds with the predator removed beside matched untouched ponds is exactly that design.
distractorNotes: This is the Yellowstone problem itself: a single before-and-after with nothing to compare it against.
A documentary is a retelling, the very thing the author warns can outrun the evidence.
One forest, one summer, and no manipulation gives nothing to compare.
A model predicts; the author wants a tested comparison, not a projection.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Wolves restored Yellowstone's willows, aspen, beavers, and rivers, confirming the cascade that Paine and Estes first described
The experiments at Mukkaw Bay and in the Aleutians showed that predators matter less than ecologists once believed
The cascade idea is sound, but Yellowstone's popular version outruns its evidence
Ecologists should abandon the term keystone species because the public misunderstands it
Elk declines in Yellowstone were caused entirely by hunters, bears, and drought rather than by wolves

proof.quote: the cleaner a cascade story sounds, the more tempting it is to tell it without checking whether every link actually held
not the strength of the idea but the shape of the evidence
whether the chain was tested or merely assumed

questions.why: Paragraph 1 sets the thesis, that clean cascade stories tempt us to skip checking the links, and paragraph 12 closes it: the idea is strong, Yellowstone's evidence is not shaped like Paine's or Estes's, and the honest way to admire the idea is to keep testing each link.
distractorNotes: This is the popular version the passage spends five paragraphs contesting.
Reversed: both experiments showed that predators matter enormously.
The author never argues against the term; it is presented approvingly.
Too strong: paragraph 12 says the wolves did not do nothing, and sorting out their share is unsolved.
